mainTopic: צדיקים are alive in death and רשעים are dead in life, and whether the dead know what happens among the living.
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining the פסוק about בניהו בן יהוידע. 'Son of a living man' means a צדיק who is called alive even after death, and his other praises describe his greatness in תורה. Then it turns to the opposite idea: רשעים are called dead even while they are alive. Next comes a story about the sons of רבי חייא, which raises the question of whether the dead know what happens to the living. The גמרא first says that the dead feel their own pain but do not know about the pain of others. It then brings three stories that seem to show the dead do know: the חסיד who slept in the cemetery, זעירי and his innkeeper, and שמואל and his father. Each proof is pushed aside, because the dead could have heard the news from someone else. Finally, the גמרא shows that רבי יונתן changed his mind. He learns from the word לֵאמֹר that משה was sent to tell the dead forefathers that God's promise was kept.

steps.title: Why call him 'son of a living man'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק calls בניהו 'son of a living man', since everyone's father was alive at some point.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Son of a living man.' Does that mean everyone else is the child of dead people?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a pointed question about an odd phrase in the פסוק describing בניהו בן יהוידע. It is setting up a new reading of the phrase.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every person is born to a living father, so calling someone 'son of a living man' seems to add nothing. The question shows that the phrase must carry a deeper meaning. The next step gives that meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? (introduces a question that sounds absurd)

phrases.english: "Son of a living man":
phrases.notes: This is from the פסוק about בניהו בן יהוידע that the גמרא was just quoting.

phrases.english: Is that to say that everyone else in the world
are children of dead men?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא בְּנֵי מֵתֵי נִינְהוּ
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain meaning of the phrase 'בן איש חי'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Everyone is born to a living father, so the description would be pointless if read literally.

steps.title: Called alive even in death
steps.stepSummary: 'Son of a living man' means a person who is called alive even after he dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, 'son of a living man' means that even in his death he is called alive.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question: the phrase describes a צדיק who stays 'alive' even after death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word חי is not about his father being alive. It describes the spiritual level of the צדיק, who is called 'living' even after he dies. This supports the larger point that צדיקים are called alive in death.
steps.whatToRemember: A צדיק is called 'alive' even after he dies.

phrases.english: Rather, "son of a living man" means
that even in his death he is called living.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בֶּן אִישׁ חַי שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ בְּמִיתָתוֹ קָרוּי חַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Son of a living man' seemed to describe his father as alive, which is true of everyone.
steps.terutzMaskana: It describes בניהו himself as one who is called alive even after death.

steps.title: He gathered many workers for תורה
steps.stepSummary: 'Great of deeds, from קבצאל' is read as: he increased and gathered workers for תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Great of deeds, from קבצאל': he increased and gathered workers for תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues through the פסוק and explains the next phrase as praise of בניהו's work for תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words are read through wordplay. רב sounds like ריבה ('increased'), and קבצאל sounds like קבץ ('gathered'). So the 'deeds' are his spreading of תורה, and the 'workers' are students.

keyTerms.meaning: Kabzeel, a place name, read here as 'gathering'
Workers, here people working in תורה

phrases.english: "Great of deeds, from Kabzeel" means
that he increased and gathered workers for the Torah.
phrases.notes: It's wordplay: רב sounds like ריבה, and קבצאל sounds like קבץ.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פְּעָלִים מִקַּבְצְאֵל שֶׁרִיבָּה וְקִבֵּץ פּוֹעֲלִים לַתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the same פסוק phrase by phrase
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'רב פעלים מקבצאל' describes בניהו increasing and gathering students of תורה.

steps.title: No one equal to him in either Temple period
steps.stepSummary: 'He struck the two אריאל of מואב' is read as: he left no one equal to him in the first or second מקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He struck the two אריאל of מואב': he left no one like him, neither in the time of the first מקדש nor in the time of the second.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the next phrase of the פסוק as a statement of how unmatched בניהו was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Struck' is read as 'surpassed', and the 'two אריאל' are read as the two בתי מקדש. So the phrase means that in neither Temple period was there anyone as great as he was.

keyTerms.meaning: Ariel, read here as a name for the בית המקדש
He left no one like him

phrases.english: "And he struck
the two Ariel of Moab" means
phrases.notes: אריאל is a name for the בית המקדש (ישעיהו 29:1), so 'two אריאל' is read as the two Temples.

phrases.english: that he did not leave anyone like him
not in the First Temple
and not in the Second Temple.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהוּא הִכָּה אֵת שְׁנֵי אֲרִאֵל מוֹאָב שֶׁלֹּא הִנִּיחַ כְּמוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues explaining the פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No one equal to בניהו existed in either Temple period.

steps.title: First reading of killing the lion: immersing in icy water
steps.stepSummary: One opinion says 'killing the lion in the pit on a snowy day' means he broke ice and went down to immerse.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He went down and killed the lion in the pit on a snowy day.' Some say: he broke blocks of ice, went down, and immersed himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the last phrase of the פסוק and gives the first of two explanations: בניהו broke through ice to immerse in a מקוה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'pit' is read as water for immersion, and 'snowy day' explains why he had to break ice. The 'lion' he defeated is the cold that stood in his way, which shows his devotion to purity.

phrases.english: "And he went down and killed the lion
inside the pit on a snowy day":
Some say:
that he broke blocks of ice,
and went down and immersed himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the last phrase of the same פסוק
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Killing the lion on a snowy day means he broke ice to immerse.

steps.title: Second reading: learning the whole ספרא on a winter day
steps.stepSummary: Another opinion says the phrase means he learned the ספרא of the school of רב on a winter day.
steps.simpleTranslation: Others say: he learned the ספרא of the school of רב on a winter day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second explanation of the same phrase: the 'lion' he defeated was the difficult ספרא, learned on a short winter day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a competing explanation of the same phrase. It reads the 'lion' as a great achievement in learning instead of in purity. This fits the theme of step 3, his greatness in תורה.

keyTerms.meaning: The ספרא of the school of רב, the halachic מדרש on ויקרא

phrases.english: Others say:
that he learned the Sifra of the school of Rav
on a winter day.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי דִּתְנָא סִיפְרָא דְבֵי רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second explanation of the same phrase
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Killing the lion on a snowy day means he mastered the ספרא on a winter day.

steps.title: רשעים are called dead even while alive
steps.stepSummary: 'The dead know nothing' refers to רשעים, who are called dead even in their lifetime, as יחזקאל calls a living king 'slain'.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'The dead know nothing' refers to the רשעים, who are called dead even while they are alive, as it says: 'And you, slain and wicked prince of ישראל.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the opposite side: just as צדיקים are alive in death, רשעים are 'dead' in life. It proves this from a פסוק in יחזקאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק 'the dead know nothing' seemed to say that the dead are unaware. The גמרא reads 'the dead' as רשעים. The proof is that יחזקאל calls a living king 'חלל', a slain person, because of his wickedness.
steps.whatToRemember: צדיקים are called alive even in death, and רשעים are called dead even in life.

phrases.english: "And the dead know nothing":
phrases.notes: קהלת 9:5

phrases.english: these are the wicked,
who even in their lifetimes are called "dead,"
as it says: "And you, slain and wicked
prince of Israel."
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 21:30

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַמֵּתִים אֵינָם יוֹדְעִים מְאוּמָה אֵלּוּ רְשָׁעִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents the mirror image of step 2
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רשעים are considered dead even while alive.

steps.title: Another proof: 'the dead shall be put to death'
steps.stepSummary: A second source: the תורה calls someone on trial 'המת' before he is executed, so a רשע is dead from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can prove it from here: 'By two or three witnesses the dead one shall be put to death.' But he is alive! Rather, he is considered dead from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another פסוק to prove that רשעים are called dead while alive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק calls the accused 'the dead one' even before his execution, while he is clearly still alive. The only way to explain this is that a רשע is already considered dead.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another proof)
The dead one shall be put to death

phrases.english: And if you want, say the proof is from here:
"By the mouth of two witnesses
or by the mouth of three witnesses
the dead one shall be put to death."
phrases.notes: דברים 17:6

phrases.english: But he is alive!
Rather, he is considered dead from the start.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, alternative proof for the claim of step 7
steps.raayaObject: That רשעים are called dead while alive
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 17:6, 'יומת המת', said about a person who is still alive

steps.title: The sons of רבי חייא forget their learning
steps.stepSummary: The sons of רבי חייא went to the villages, forgot their learning, and struggled to recall it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The sons of רבי חייא went out to the villages. Their learning became hard for them to remember, and they were struggling to recall it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story connected to the question of whether the dead know what happens to the living. This step sets the scene.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sons are away from the בית מדרש, lose hold of their תלמוד, and are pained by it. Their distress leads to the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Became heavy, became hard to hold onto

phrases.english: The sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya went out to the villages.
Their learning became heavy for them.
phrases.notes: Literally 'heavy' or 'hard'. It means they forgot what they had learned.

phrases.english: They were straining in distress to recall it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a story about whether the dead are aware of the living
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setting of the story: the sons are pained at forgetting their learning.

steps.title: Does our father know of our pain?
steps.stepSummary: One son asks his brother whether their late father knows of their distress.
steps.simpleTranslation: One said to the other: Does our father know about this distress?
steps.whatsHappening: Inside the story, one brother asks whether the dead, here their father רבי חייא, are aware of what happens to their children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This raises the real question of the passage: do the dead know about the living? The answer comes in the next step.

phrases.english: One said to the other:
Does our father know about this distress?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story with the central question
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the dead know about the suffering of the living

steps.title: How would he know? The dead do not know
steps.stepSummary: The other brother answers from a פסוק in איוב that the dead do not know what happens to their children.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other said to him: How would he know? It is written: 'His sons are honored and he does not know.'
steps.whatsHappening: The second brother answers that their father cannot know, and quotes a פסוק to prove it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in איוב says that a dead man does not know whether his children are honored. So the dead seem unaware of the living. This answer will be tested as the story continues.

phrases.english: The other one said to him: From where would he know?
Isn't it written:
"His sons are honored, and he does not know"?
phrases.notes: איוב 14:21

steps.triggerLanguage: מְנָא יָדַע וְהָא כְּתִיב יִכְבְּדוּ בָנָיו וְלֹא יֵדָע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the brother's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The dead do not know, based on איוב 14:21.

steps.title: The other brother objects: the dead do feel things
steps.stepSummary: The other brother challenges the claim that the dead know nothing. He quotes a פסוק in איוב and רבי יצחק's teaching that worms hurt the dead like a needle hurts the living.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other said to him: Do the dead really not know? It is written: 'Only his flesh feels pain, and his soul mourns.' And רבי יצחק said: a worm is as painful to the dead as a needle in living flesh!
steps.whatsHappening: The other brother pushes back on the answer from Step 11. He brings a פסוק showing that the dead can feel pain, so they must be aware of something.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 said the dead do not know anything. This step argues that if a dead body feels the worms, the dead clearly have some awareness. So the claim 'they know nothing' cannot be fully true.

keyTerms.meaning: The other one (here, the other brother)
But isn't it written: an opening for a challenge from a פסוק
Worm or maggot that eats a dead body

phrases.english: The other said to him:
And does he not know?
But isn't it written:
"Only his flesh upon him feels pain,
phrases.notes: איוב 14:22

phrases.english: and his soul upon him mourns."
And Rabbi Yitzchak said:
A worm is as painful to the dead
as a needle in living flesh!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אִידַּךְ: וְלָא יָדַע? וְהָא כְּתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 11 that the dead know nothing.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim from Step 11 that the dead know nothing at all.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק and רבי יצחק show the dead feel the pain of worms, so they do have some awareness.

steps.title: The dead know their own pain but not the pain of others
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא settles the conflict: the dead feel their own suffering, but they do not know about other people's suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: About their own pain, the dead know. About the pain of others, they do not know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by splitting the question into two kinds of knowing. The dead feel what happens to them, but not what happens to others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about worms talks about the dead person's own body. The פסוק from Step 11 talks about the dead not knowing about their children. So both פסוקים can be true: the dead feel their own pain but not other people's.

phrases.english: They said:
Of their own pain, they know;
of the pain of others, they do not know.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of Step 12 by drawing a distinction.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between two kinds of knowledge
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed the פסוקים conflict: one says the dead know nothing, the other says they feel pain.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dead feel their own pain but do not know about the pain of others.

steps.title: A challenge from a ברייתא: the חסיד who slept in the cemetery
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the dead really don't know about others, and begins a ברייתא about a חסיד who gave charity, was provoked by his wife, and went to sleep in a cemetery.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do they really not know? But it was taught: There was a story with a pious man who gave a dinar to a poor man on ערב ראש השנה during years of drought. His wife provoked him, so he went and slept in the cemetery.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 13 and starts telling a story to prove its point. This step only sets up the story; the proof comes in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 13 said the dead don't know about what happens to others. The גמרא now brings a ברייתא that seems to show dead spirits who do know about the world. Here we only meet the main character and learn why he ended up in a cemetery.

phrases.english: And do they not? But wasn't it taught:
An incident with a certain pious man
who gave a dinar to a poor man
on the eve of Rosh Hashanah
in years of drought,
and his wife provoked him,
and he went and slept in the cemetery.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction made in Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in Step 13 that the dead do not know about matters beyond themselves.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא tells of dead spirits who seek out and learn what will happen in the world, which seems to show the dead do know about others.

steps.title: First year: the spirits warn of hail and the חסיד saves his crop
steps.stepSummary: The חסיד overhears two spirits. One goes to listen behind the heavenly curtain and learns that hail will strike whoever sows in the first rainfall. He sows in the second and his crop is saved.
steps.simpleTranslation: He heard two spirits talking. One said: Come, let us roam the world and hear from behind the curtain what calamity is coming. The other said: I can't, I'm buried in a mat of reeds; you go and tell me. She went and came back and said: Anyone who sows in the first rainfall will be struck by hail. He sowed in the second rainfall. Everyone's crops were struck, but his were not.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the first part of the story that proves the challenge. Dead spirits talk about and learn what will happen in the world, and the חסיד benefits from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The spirits are dead, yet they want to know what calamity is coming to the world and can find out. That seems to go against the idea that the dead don't know about matters beyond themselves. The חסיד's saved crop shows the information was true.

keyTerms.meaning: The heavenly curtain, behind which decrees are heard
A rainfall season, a time for planting

phrases.english: And he heard two spirits
talking to each other.
One said to her friend:
My friend, come, let us roam the world,
and hear from behind the curtain
phrases.notes: This is the heavenly curtain; behind it you can hear what is being decreed for the world.

phrases.english: what calamity is coming to the world.
Her friend said to her:
I cannot,
because I am buried in a mat of reeds.
Rather, you go,
and what you hear, tell me.
She went, roamed, and came back.
And her friend said to her:
My friend, what did you hear from behind the curtain?
She said to her:
I heard that anyone who sows in the first rainfall
hail will strike him.
He went and sowed in the second rainfall.
The crops of the whole world were struck,
his were not struck.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְשָׁמַע שְׁתֵּי רוּחוֹת שֶׁמְסַפְּרוֹת זוֹ לָזוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא begun in Step 14, giving the content that powers the challenge.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead can know about what happens in the world beyond themselves.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the חסיד who overheard two spirits in the cemetery.

steps.title: Second year: the spirits warn of blight and the חסיד saves his crop again
steps.stepSummary: The next year the חסיד returns to the cemetery. The spirits repeat their conversation, and this time learn that blight will strike whoever sows in the second rainfall. He sows in the first and his crop is saved again.
steps.simpleTranslation: The next year he slept in the cemetery again and heard the same two spirits. One asked the other to come roam the world. The other said: Didn't I tell you I can't, since I'm buried in a mat of reeds? You go and tell me. She went and came back and said: Anyone who sows in the second rainfall will be struck by blight. He sowed in the first rainfall. Everyone's crops were blighted, but his were not.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues with a second year that mirrors the first. Again the spirits learn about a coming calamity, and the חסיד uses it to protect his crop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This time he went to the cemetery on purpose, not because his wife provoked him. Once again the dead spirits know what is coming to the world, which strengthens the challenge against Step 13. The story is not finished yet and continues after this.

keyTerms.meaning: Blight: crops dried out by a hot wind

steps.confusionAlert: Notice the switch: in the first year the danger was in the first rainfall, so he sowed in the second. In the second year the danger was in the second rainfall, so he sowed in the first.

phrases.english: The next year
he went and slept in the cemetery,
and heard those two spirits
talking with each other.
One said to her friend:
Come, let us roam the world
and hear from behind the curtain
what calamity is coming to the world.
She said to her:
My friend, did I not already tell you:
I cannot,
because I am buried in a mat of reeds?!
Rather, you go,

phrases.aramaic: וּמַה שֶּׁאַתְּ שׁוֹמַעַת בּוֹאִי וְאִמְרִי לִי.
phrases.english: and what you hear, come and tell me.
She went, roamed, and came back.
And her friend said to her:
My friend, what did you hear from behind the curtain?
She said to her:
I heard that anyone who sows in the second rainfall
blight will strike him.
He went and sowed in the first rainfall,
the crops of the whole world were blighted
and his were not blighted.

steps.triggerLanguage: לַשָּׁנָה הָאַחֶרֶת הָלַךְ וְלָן בְּבֵית הַקְּבָרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a second year that mirrors the first.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know about what is coming to the world.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The second year of the ברייתא of the חסיד in the cemetery.

steps.title: The wife finds out and taunts the girl's mother
steps.stepSummary: The חסיד's wife asks why only his crops survived. He tells her everything, and she later taunts the dead girl's mother that her daughter is buried in a reed mat.
steps.simpleTranslation: His wife asked him: Why last year was everyone's crop struck and yours was not, and this year everyone's crop was blighted and yours was not? He told her the whole story. Within a few days a fight broke out between his wife and the mother of the dead girl. His wife said to her: Come, I'll show you your daughter, buried in a mat of reeds.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. The secret of the cemetery conversation now gets out into the world of the living, and this sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The important detail is that the living now know what the spirits said, including that the girl was buried in a reed mat. This is what will let the spirits find out that they were overheard.

keyTerms.meaning: was blighted, dried out by wind

phrases.english: His wife said to him:
Why is it that last year
the crops of the whole world were struck
and yours were not struck,

phrases.aramaic: וְעַכְשָׁיו שֶׁל כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ נִשְׁדַּף
phrases.english: and now the crops of the whole world were blighted
and yours were not blighted?
He told her all these things.
They said: not even a few days passed
before a quarrel broke out
between the wife of that pious man
and the mother of that young girl.
She said to her: Go, and I will show you your daughter,
that she is buried in a mat of reeds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from step 16. It shows how the spirits' secret leaked to the living.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know what happens among the living
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of the חסיד in the cemetery

steps.title: The spirits know they were overheard
steps.stepSummary: The next year, one spirit refuses to go listen behind the curtain because their private words were already heard among the living. The גמרא concludes that the dead know.
steps.simpleTranslation: The next year he again slept in the cemetery and heard the spirits talking. One said: My friend, come, let us roam the world and hear from behind the curtain what disaster is coming. The other said: My friend, leave me alone. What we said between us has already been heard among the living. So the dead know!
steps.whatsHappening: The story finishes, and the גמרא draws its point: the dead do know what goes on in this world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The spirit knew about something that happened only among the living, the wife's taunt. This seems to contradict step 13, which said the dead don't know about other people's affairs.

phrases.english: The following year
he went and slept in the cemetery
and heard those spirits
talking with each other.
One said to the other: My friend,
come, let us roam the world
and hear from behind the curtain
what disaster is coming to the world.
She said to her: My friend, leave me alone,
the words between me and you
have already been heard among the living.
Apparently, they know.
phrases.notes: Now the גמרא is talking, not the spirit. The dead know what happens here.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא and draws the proof that step 14 was building toward.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know about events among the living, against the answer in step 13
steps.raayaSupportSource: The spirit knew the conversation had been heard among the living

steps.title: Maybe someone who died later told them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. Perhaps another person died afterward, arrived in the cemetery, and told the spirits.
steps.simpleTranslation: Maybe someone else died, came, and told them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: the story does not prove that the dead can see what happens among the living.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The spirits may not have known on their own. A newly dead person could have brought the news, so the answer of step 13 can still stand.

phrases.english: Perhaps another person died,
and went and told them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof drawn in step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the ברייתא of the חסיד
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The spirits' knowledge could have come from a newly dead person, not from seeing the living world directly.

steps.title: The dead innkeeper tells זעירי where his money is
steps.stepSummary: זעירי's innkeeper died while holding his money. At her grave she told him where it was and asked her mother to send her things with a woman who would die the next day. This shows the dead know.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: זעירי used to leave his money with his innkeeper. While he was going back and forth to רב's study hall, she died. He went to her grave and asked: Where is the money? She said: Go take it from under the door hinge in such-and-such a place. And tell my mother to send me my comb and my tube of eye-paint with so-and-so, who is coming here tomorrow. So the dead know!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new proof that the dead know what happens among the living.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the dead woman knew something no newly dead person could have told her: which living woman would die tomorrow. So the answer of step 19 does not work here, and this again challenges step 13.
steps.whatToRemember: The חסיד story was pushed aside. The story of זעירי now seems to show that the dead know what happens among the living. The next step pushes this proof aside too.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
For זעירי used to deposit coins
with his innkeeper.
While he was coming and going to the house of Rav,
phrases.notes: He means רב's study hall.

phrases.english: she died.
He went after her to the cemetery,
he said to her: Where are the coins?
She said to him: Go take them
from under the hinge of the door
in such-and-such a place,
and tell my mother
to send me my comb
and my tube of eye-paint
with so-and-so
who is coming tomorrow.
phrases.notes: She means a woman who will die tomorrow and arrive in the cemetery.

phrases.english: Apparently, they know!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: דִּזְעֵירִי הֲוָה מַפְקֵיד זוּזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 19 rejected the first proof, this brings a new proof for the same point.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know what happens among the living
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of זעירי and his dead innkeeper

steps.title: Maybe the angel דומה announced it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from זעירי's innkeeper. Perhaps the angel דומה announces ahead of time who is going to die.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps דומה comes first and announces it to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the innkeeper story. The dead may not know anything on their own. An angel may simply tell them who is coming.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the last proof, the dead innkeeper knew that a certain woman would die the next day. The גמרא says this doesn't prove the dead know things by themselves. דומה, the angel in charge of the dead, could have told them who was about to arrive.

keyTerms.meaning: The angel in charge of the dead

phrases.english: Perhaps דומה
phrases.notes: דומה is the angel who watches over the dead.

phrases.english: comes beforehand and announces it to them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 20.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Knowing who will die tomorrow could come from an angel's announcement. It does not have to come from the dead's own knowledge.

steps.title: שמואל searches the cemetery for his father
steps.stepSummary: A new proof begins. שמואל's father died while holding orphans' money, and nobody knew where it was. שמואל goes to the cemetery to ask him and is told that his father has gone up to the heavenly yeshiva.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: People left orphans' money with שמואל's father. When he died, שמואל was not with him, and people called שמואל 'son of the one who ate orphans' money.' שמואל went to the cemetery and asked for אבא. They said there were many named אבא, and many named אבא בר אבא. When he asked for אבא בר אבא, father of שמואל, they told him he had gone up to the heavenly yeshiva.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story to prove that the dead know things. This part sets the scene: why שמואל went to the cemetery and what he was told there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story has to explain why שמואל needed his dead father. Nobody knew where the orphans' money was, so שמואל's good name was at stake. The real proof comes later in the story, when his father speaks to him.

keyTerms.meaning: Cemetery, literally the courtyard of death

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲבוּהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל הֲווֹ קָא מַפְקְדִי גַּבֵּיהּ
phrases.english: With שמואל's father, people would deposit
the money of orphans.
When he died,
שמואל was not with him.
People were calling him:
'Son of the one who eats orphans' money.'
He went after him to the cemetery.
He said to them: I want Abba!
phrases.notes: His father's name was אבא. שמואל is speaking to the dead.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: אַבָּא טוּבָא אִיכָּא הָכָא.
phrases.english: They said to him: There are many Abbas here.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: בָּעֵינָא אַבָּא בַּר אַבָּא.
phrases.english: He said to them: I want Abba bar Abba.
They said to him: Abba bar Abba,
there are also many here.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: בָּעֵינָא אַבָּא בַּר אַבָּא
phrases.english: He said to them: I want Abba bar Abba,
the father of שמואל. Where is he?
They said to him: He went up to the heavenly yeshiva.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: דַּאֲבוּהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל הֲווֹ קָא מַפְקְדִי גַּבֵּיהּ זוּזֵי דְיַתְמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof in step 20 was rejected, a new proof begins.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know what goes on among the living
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of שמואל and his father's orphans' money

steps.title: לוי sits outside the heavenly yeshiva
steps.stepSummary: While waiting, שמואל sees his friend לוי sitting outside. לוי explains that he is kept out because he upset רבי אפס by not attending his yeshiva.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile, שמואל saw לוי sitting outside and asked why he hadn't gone up. לוי said: They tell me that because for all those years I didn't attend רבי אפס's yeshiva and upset him, they won't let me into the heavenly yeshiva.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues with a side scene about שמואל's friend לוי. This sets up what happens when שמואל's father arrives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This part does not prove anything about the dead yet. It sets up a later moment, when שמואל uses his importance to get לוי admitted.

keyTerms.meaning: The head of a yeshiva in his generation
You upset him, literally you weakened his mind

phrases.english: Meanwhile, he saw לוי sitting outside.
He said to him: Why are you sitting outside?
Why didn't you go up?
He said to him: Because they tell me:
All those years
that you did not go to the yeshiva of רבי אפס
and you upset him,
we will not let you into the heavenly yeshiva.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story begun in step 22.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know what goes on among the living
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of שמואל in the cemetery (side scene with לוי)

steps.title: The father cries and laughs
steps.stepSummary: שמואל's father arrives crying and laughing. He cries because שמואל will soon die, and laughs because שמואל is very important. שמואל uses his importance to get לוי admitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile his father came. שמואל saw him crying and laughing and asked why he was crying. He said: Because you are coming here soon. Why was he laughing? Because you are very important in this world. שמואל said: If I am important, let them bring לוי in. And they brought לוי in.
steps.whatsHappening: The father finally appears and reveals that he knows שמואל will die soon. This is the heart of the proof that the dead know things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father knows something about the future of a living person, that שמואל will die soon. He also knows how important שמואל is. שמואל was not dying the next day, so this does not look like a simple announcement by דומה about tomorrow's arrivals.

phrases.english: Meanwhile, his father came,
and he saw that he was crying and laughing.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי טַעְמָא קָא בָכֵית?
phrases.english: He said to him: Why are you crying?
He said to him: Because you are coming here soon.
Why are you laughing?
Because you are very important in this world.
phrases.notes: Literally 'this world'. The words alone don't say which world he means.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי חֲשִׁיבְנָא — נְעַיְּילוּהּ לְלֵוִי.
phrases.english: He said to him: If I am important, let them bring לוי in.
And they brought לוי in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story. The father arrives, and the לוי side scene is resolved.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know what goes on among the living
steps.raayaSupportSource: The father's knowledge that שמואל will soon die

steps.title: Finding the orphans' money, and the conclusion
steps.stepSummary: The father tells שמואל that the money is hidden in the millhouse, with the orphans' money in the middle to protect it. The גמרא concludes that the dead know.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל asked: Where is the orphans' money? He said: Go take it from the millhouse. The top and bottom coins are ours, and the middle ones belong to the orphans. Why did you do this? If thieves steal, they steal from ours. If the ground rots it, it rots ours. So we see that the dead know!
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the money found and שמואל's name cleared. Then the גמרא states its conclusion: the dead know.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father placed his own money on top and bottom, so any loss would come from his money and not from the orphans'. The proof itself is the father's knowledge that שמואל would die soon (step 24). The גמרא sums it up with אלמא, 'so we see.'

keyTerms.meaning: The top ones and the bottom ones

steps.whatToRemember: The father knew that שמואל would die soon. This seems to show that the dead know what happens among the living.

phrases.english: He said to him: Where is the orphans' money?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: זִיל שַׁקְלִינְהוּ בְּאַמְתָא דְרִחְיָא.
phrases.english: He said to him: Go take it from the millhouse.
The top and the bottom ones are ours,
and the middle ones belong to the orphans.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי טַעְמָא עֲבַדְתְּ הָכִי?
phrases.english: He said to him: Why did you do it this way?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי גָּנְבִי גַּנָּבֵי — מִגַּנְבוּ מִדִּידַן.
phrases.english: He said to him: If thieves steal, they will steal from ours.
phrases.notes: A thief grabs the top coins first, and those were his own.

phrases.english: If the ground eats away at it, it will eat from ours.
phrases.notes: Damp ground ruins the bottom coins first, and those were also his own.

phrases.english: So we see that they know!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story and draws the conclusion from it.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead know what goes on among the living
steps.raayaSupportSource: The whole story of שמואל and his father, especially the father's knowledge that שמואל would die soon

steps.title: Maybe שמואל is different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. שמואל is so important that his coming is announced in advance, so this does not show that the dead know things in general.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps שמואל is different. Since he is important, they announce ahead of time: Make room!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from שמואל's father. The father may have known only because שמואל's arrival was announced.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof depended on the father knowing that שמואל would die soon, even though it was not the next day. The גמרא answers that an important person like שמואל gets a special early announcement. That does not show that the dead normally know such things.
steps.whatToRemember: All three proofs are pushed aside. In each case the dead could have heard the news from someone else: a newly dead person (the חסיד story, step 19), the angel דומה (זעירי's innkeeper, step 21), or a special announcement for an important person like שמואל (step 26).

phrases.english: Perhaps שמואל is different,

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דַּחֲשִׁיב קָדְמִי וּמַכְרְזִי: פַּנּוּ מָקוֹם.
phrases.english: since he is important, they announce ahead of time: Make room!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the conclusion drawn in step 25.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: שמואל is a special case. His coming was announced early because of his importance, so the story says nothing about ordinary dead people knowing things.

steps.title: רבי יונתן changes his mind and brings a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says that רבי יונתן also came around and agreed that the dead are aware. It proves this from his own teaching that the dead talk with one another, based on a פסוק in דברים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even רבי יונתן changed his mind. רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: How do we know that the dead talk with each other? Because the פסוק says: "And ה׳ said to him: This is the land that I swore to אברהם, יצחק and יעקב, saying."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says that רבי יונתן, who earlier held that the dead know nothing, changed his mind. It quotes his own teaching that the dead talk to each other, and starts quoting the פסוק that proves it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי יונתן was the main voice saying the dead know nothing. Here his own statement shows he later held the dead can talk and be told things. The proof will rest on the last word of the פסוק, לֵאמֹר, which the גמרא explains in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: He went back on his words; he changed his mind
From where do we know? (asks for a source)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי יונתן is arguing against himself here. The גמרא is saying he changed his earlier view, and this later teaching shows his new position.
steps.whyThisMatters: The opinion that seemed most firmly against the idea that the dead know now turns out to support it. This changes the balance of the whole סוגיא.

phrases.english: And even Rabbi Yonatan changed his mind,
phrases.notes: Earlier in the סוגיא, רבי יונתן said the dead know nothing. 'Even' means he too came to agree that they do know.

phrases.english: as Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
From where do we know that the dead
talk with one another?
As it says: "And ה׳ said to him,
phrases.notes: דברים 34:4. 'Him' is משה, just before he dies.

phrases.english: This is the land that I swore
to Avraham, to Yitzchak and to Yaakov, saying."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן הֲדַר בֵּיהּ, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from שמואל was rejected in Step 26, the גמרא adds that in any case רבי יונתן, the main voice against the idea, changed his mind and held that the dead talk with one another.
steps.raayaObject: That the dead are aware and talk with one another
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יונתן's own teaching based on דברים 34:4
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Even רבי יונתן retracted his earlier claim that the dead know nothing. He holds that the dead at least talk with one another and can be told news.

steps.title: What does the word "saying" mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the extra word לֵאמֹר ('saying') in the פסוק is teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the meaning of "saying"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא focuses on the last word of the פסוק and asks what it means. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually לֵאמֹר means 'saying' or 'in order to tell someone.' Here it seems unclear who is supposed to be told, so the גמרא asks what message it refers to and who should hear it.

phrases.english: What is "saying"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Zooms in on the key word of the פסוק quoted in Step 27.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the word לֵאמֹר adds to the פסוק

steps.title: משה is sent to tell the forefathers
steps.stepSummary: "Saying" means that הקב״ה told משה to go and tell אברהם, יצחק and יעקב that He had kept His oath to their children. Since the forefathers were already dead, this shows that the dead can be told things and talk with each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: הקב״ה said to משה: Go tell אברהם, יצחק and יעקב: The oath that I swore to you, I have already kept for your children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that לֵאמֹר means 'go and say': משה is told to bring a message to the forefathers. This finishes רבי יונתן's proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אברהם, יצחק and יעקב had died long before. If משה, who was about to die, is sent to tell them news, then the dead can receive messages and talk among themselves. That is exactly what רבי יונתן set out to prove.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He
An oath; a promise made with an oath
I have kept it; I have carried it out

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יונתן learns from לֵאמֹר that משה was sent to tell the dead forefathers that the promise was kept. So even רבי יונתן agrees that the dead talk with each other and can be told things.

phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moshe:
Go and tell them,
Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov:
The oath that I swore to you
I have already kept for your children.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה: לֵךְ אֱמוֹר לָהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 28 and completes the proof begun in Step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: לֵאמֹר means 'go and say': משה is sent to tell the dead forefathers that the oath has been kept, which shows the dead can receive messages and talk with each other.
